howItWorks.intro: This estimate multiplies a national-average base premium by an age-rating factor modeled on the ACA's permitted 3:1 age curve and a family-size factor that adds each covered member's individually-rated premium, then subtracts an estimated premium tax credit based on how your income compares to the federal poverty level. It's a simplified stand-in for the county-by-county underwriting math insurers and healthcare.gov actually run.

rules.name: Premium
rules.formula: Premium = Base × Age Factor × Family Size Factor - Subsidy
rules.explanation: Adjusted base premium minus any applicable subsidies.

howItWorks.outro: Because this calculator can't see your ZIP code, your insurers' actual filed rates, or this year's official poverty guidelines, treat the output as a starting point for budgeting — not a bindable rate. Real premiums are filed per county rating area and reset every plan year, so confirm numbers on healthcare.gov, your state's exchange, or with a licensed agent before you enroll.

faq.question: Do I qualify for a subsidy?
faq.answer: Historically, households with MAGI roughly between 100% and 400% of the federal poverty level have qualified for premium tax credits, and enhanced-credit rules have at times extended eligibility above 400% by capping the benchmark Silver premium as a share of income instead of a hard cutoff. Because these thresholds and enhancement rules are set by legislation and change over time, confirm current eligibility on healthcare.gov rather than relying on any single percentage.

faq.question: What plan tier should I choose?
faq.answer: Bronze suits someone who rarely sees a doctor and mainly wants protection from catastrophic costs — premiums are low, deductibles are high. Silver is worth a close look if your income qualifies you for cost-sharing reductions, since it can quietly beat Gold on real out-of-pocket costs. Gold and Platinum tend to pay off if you expect regular prescriptions, specialist visits, or a planned procedure, where the higher premium is offset by much lower deductibles and copays.

faq.question: Why does my age change the premium so much?
faq.answer: ACA rules let insurers charge their oldest enrollees (64) up to three times what they charge a 21-year-old for the identical plan. That ratio phases in gradually with each birthday rather than jumping at a single threshold, which is why the age factor is usually the biggest single driver of the estimate once you're past your late 40s.

faq.question: Why doesn't this ask for my state or ZIP code?
faq.answer: Because real premiums are filed by insurers per county rating area and change annually, an enrollable quote requires pulling live plan data for your exact location. This calculator applies national-average pricing scaled by age, family size, and tier, so use the dollar figures as a planning baseline and pull your real number from healthcare.gov or your state exchange.

faq.question: Is this the same as pricing an employer health plan?
faq.answer: No. Employer-sponsored premiums are priced across your company's whole risk pool and usually include an employer contribution this tool doesn't model. This calculator estimates individual marketplace pricing, which insurers price per person by age, tobacco use, and location — COBRA continuation coverage, by contrast, typically costs the full unsubsidized group rate plus a 2% administrative fee.

faq.question: How accurate is this estimate?
faq.answer: It's built for budgeting and side-by-side comparison, not enrollment. Real premiums depend on your specific insurer, county, plan design, and the current year's official poverty guidelines and subsidy formulas, all of which shift year to year. Before enrolling, verify pricing directly on healthcare.gov, your state's exchange, or with a licensed agent.

howWeCalculate.intro: The estimate runs in three layers: a base monthly premium standing in for an average-cost plan nationally, an age multiplier drawn from the ACA's permitted 3:1 rating curve, and a family-size multiplier that adds each additional covered person's individually-rated premium — a couple pays roughly double a single adult's rate, not the flat per-person number a simpler calculator might suggest.
steps: Your annual income is compared against the federal poverty level for your household size to estimate what share of income you'd be expected to contribute toward a benchmark Silver plan
Your age is run through the ACA's 3:1 age curve to scale the base premium up or down — this is usually the single biggest lever in the estimate for adults over 50
Family size adds an individually-rated premium for each additional household member, since insurers price dependents one at a time rather than applying a flat headcount multiplier
Your selected plan tier adjusts the base premium by its actuarial-value band, then the estimated subsidy is subtracted to produce the net monthly and annual figures shown
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: This model uses national averages and simplified age and subsidy curves — it doesn't know your state, county rating area, insurer network, or the current year's official poverty guidelines. For an enrollable quote, use healthcare.gov, your state's exchange, or a licensed insurance agent.

whenToUse.intro: A premium estimate is most useful before you're staring down a real enrollment deadline. A few situations where running these numbers actually helps:
scenarios: Comparing a COBRA offer against marketplace pricing after a layoff, before your COBRA election window closes
Estimating whether a part-time or freelance income shift mid-year would change your subsidy eligibility
Deciding between a high-deductible Bronze plan paired with an HSA and a lower-deductible Silver plan before open enrollment starts
Sanity-checking a healthcare.gov quote that looks unusually high or low for your age and income
Modeling how adding a spouse or dependent to your policy changes the household premium versus keeping separate coverage

sections.title: Metal Tiers: The Premium-vs-Deductible Tradeoff
sections.body: The ACA marketplace sorts every plan into one of four metal tiers — Bronze, Silver, Gold, or Platinum — based on actuarial value, not on plan quality. Actuarial value is the average share of covered costs the insurer pays for a standard population: roughly 60% for Bronze, 70% for Silver, 80% for Gold, and 90% for Platinum. The plan covers that percentage; you cover the rest through deductibles, copays, and coinsurance. That's why Bronze premiums run lowest while individual deductibles often clear $7,000, and why Platinum premiums run highest while deductibles can sit under $500. Silver occupies the middle and carries one extra feature the others don't: it's the only tier eligible for cost-sharing reductions (CSRs), which shrink out-of-pocket maximums for households under roughly 250% of the federal poverty level — which is why advisors often steer lower-income shoppers toward Silver even when Bronze looks cheaper on the sticker price.

sections.title: Why Two People the Same Age Pay Different Premiums
sections.body: Federal rules restrict insurers to varying individual-market premiums by only three factors: age, tobacco use, and geographic rating area — never health status, gender, or pre-existing conditions. Age pricing follows a published curve; insurers can charge their oldest enrollees (64) up to three times what they charge a 21-year-old for the identical plan, and this calculator's age factor mirrors that curve, which is why premiums climb noticeably faster once you're past your late 40s. Rating area is usually tied to county and reflects local hospital and provider costs — a Bronze plan in a rural county can differ from the same metal tier in a nearby metro area by well over $100/month at the same age. States can also layer stricter rules on top of the federal floor: New York and Vermont use pure community rating with no age variation at all, while most states use the full 3:1 band. Because this tool has no way to know your county, treat its base premium as a national-average starting point, not a locked-in rate for your area.

sections.title: A Worked Example: Age 45, $42,000 Income, Household of One
sections.body: Say you're 45, single, and expect roughly $42,000 in modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) for the coverage year. Illustrative, non-quoted premiums might show a benchmark Silver plan (the second-lowest-cost Silver plan in an area, used to calculate subsidies) at $610/month and a comparable Bronze plan at $480/month. If your income puts your required contribution toward the benchmark plan at around 6% of MAGI — about $210/month in this example — your estimated premium tax credit would be the difference: roughly $400/month. Apply that same $400 credit to the cheaper Bronze plan and your net cost drops to about $80/month with a high deductible; apply it to the benchmark Silver plan instead and you'd pay closer to $210/month with meaningfully lower out-of-pocket costs if you also qualify for cost-sharing reductions. Every number here is illustrative — your real benchmark premium depends entirely on which insurers filed plans in your county for that plan year.

sections.title: Employer Coverage vs. the Marketplace
sections.body: If you have access to an employer plan that's considered affordable (employee-only premium under a federally set percentage of income) and meets minimum value standards, you generally won't qualify for marketplace subsidies even if you decline it and shop the exchange instead. This calculator models individual marketplace pricing only — it doesn't reflect employer group-rate premiums, which are priced across your whole company's risk pool rather than by individual age, or COBRA continuation coverage, which typically costs the full unsubsidized group premium plus a 2% administrative fee.

howToSteps.title: Enter Your Annual Income
howToSteps.description: Use your expected modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) for the coverage year, not last year's W-2 total. Self-employed users and retirees especially should estimate forward, since this figure drives the subsidy portion of the result.

howToSteps.title: Enter Your Age and Family Size
howToSteps.description: Age feeds directly into the ACA's age-rating curve. Family size should reflect your tax household — the people you'd claim on your return — since that determines both the poverty-level comparison and the per-person premium add-ons.

howToSteps.title: Select a Plan Tier
howToSteps.description: Bronze trades a low premium for a high deductible (about 60% actuarial value); Gold and Platinum flip that ratio toward higher premiums and lower out-of-pocket costs. If you're unsure, Silver is the only tier that unlocks cost-sharing reductions for qualifying incomes.

howToSteps.title: Review the Premium and Subsidy Breakdown
howToSteps.description: The subsidy figure is an estimated premium tax credit; the monthly and annual premiums shown are household totals, not per-person amounts. Compare the net numbers across tiers before deciding where to shop first.

tips: Enter modified adjusted gross income (MAGI), not gross wages — self-employment deductions, pre-tax retirement contributions, and above-the-line deductions all reduce MAGI and can change the subsidy estimate meaningfully.
If you're under 30, or qualify for a hardship exemption, catastrophic plans exist outside these four metal tiers and aren't modeled here — very low premiums, but no subsidy eligibility.

Only Bronze and some Silver plans typically qualify as HSA-eligible high-deductible health plans; a Gold or Platinum plan generally won't let you contribute to an HSA even with a comparatively high deductible.
Silver is the only tier where cost-sharing reductions apply, so two Silver quotes at the same premium can carry very different real-world deductibles depending on household income.
For subsidy purposes, family size means your tax household, not just the people on the policy — dependents you claim still count even if they're covered elsewhere.
